title: The standing prayer
hook: Ardas is prayed standing, hands folded, at the start and end of everything

segments.voice: Yesterday: nirbhau, and your line: calm and fearless. Which salok did you choose to carry this week? Today a new block begins: the Ardas, line by line. Day six hundred eleven.

At the end of a gurdwara service, the whole room does the same thing. Everyone who was sitting cross-legged on the floor gets up. They stand, face the Guru Granth Sahib, and fold their hands in front of them. One person starts speaking, steady and rhythmic, and every so often the whole room answers in one word: Waheguru. You'll see the same thing at a wedding, before a new business opens, before a long journey, beside a hospital bed, at a funeral. Before a meal is served from the langar, and after. It's the Sikh prayer for everything. Today: the standing prayer.
screen: `THE WHOLE ROOM STANDS.` → `HANDS FOLDED, FACING THE GURU.` → `THE PRAYER FOR EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: It's called Ardas. Sikh tradition explains the word through the Persian arz-dasht: a petition, a written request, the kind handed up to a king. Heard that way, the name says what the Ardas is. It's a petition to God, made standing, the way you'd stand before someone you honor. It isn't one of the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib. It grew up in the community, and its standard form is set out in the Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada. Over the coming weeks we'll go through it line by line. For now, here's the shape. It has three movements. First, it opens with lines from Guru Gobind Singh's Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki, remembering God's power and the Gurus by name. Second, it remembers: the Guru Granth Sahib, the Panj Pyare, the Sahibzade, the martyrs, the gurdwaras, the long history of the community. Third, it asks: for the Name, for faith, for the good of the whole Khalsa, and then for whatever this particular moment needs, a wedding, a journey, a recovery. Then it closes by asking for the good of everyone. Notice that order. Before asking for anything, the Ardas remembers. By the time the request comes, you've been reminded who you stand with. And the room keeps answering, Waheguru, so the prayer is never one person's alone. The opening and the remembering stay much the same everywhere. The ask at the end changes with the occasion. That's why it can stand at the start and end of everything. It carries the whole history of the community, and room for this one Tuesday.
screen: `ARDAS: A PETITION, MADE STANDING.` · `FIRST, IT OPENS WITH THE GURUS.` · `NEXT, IT REMEMBERS THE COMMUNITY.` · `LAST, IT ASKS, FOR TODAY TOO.` · then, large: `STAND AND ASK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand for one minute's prayer, or one minute's quiet. If you can, get up. Stand with your feet steady and fold your hands in front of you. Notice whether standing feels different from sitting, as if someone were in front of you. If you pray, you can ask God for one thing you need today, in your own plain words, and end with Waheguru. If you don't, stand and name, silently, one thing you hope for, for yourself and for someone else. The bell holds the time.
Ardas. A petition, made standing with folded hands: first it remembers, then it asks.
Your line: stand and ask. Before one thing you begin today, stand still for a breath and name what you hope for. Day six hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Sikhs say the Ardas standing with folded hands, facing the Guru Granth Sahib where it is present, at the end of services and at the start and end of any important undertaking, with the sangat answering Waheguru.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Ardas, the standing petition; tradition explains the word through Persian arz-dasht, a written request.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ardas is just the Sikh word for prayer.
what it means: it's a petition, made standing, that remembers before it asks.
what a scholar hears: the Persian arz-dasht was a petition submitted to a ruler; the Ardas opens with Guru Gobind Singh's Var Sri Bhagauti Ji Ki, and its standard text is set by the Rehat Maryada.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): replaced the banned 'Walk into any gurdwara' opener; the Persian arz-dasht origin is now told as how Sikh tradition explains the word; 'next five weeks' became 'coming weeks'; the Var stanza remembers the Gurus, not 'the ten Gurus' (the tenth is added in the Ardas itself); the practice no longer tells the listener how standing feels.
Etymology of Ardas from Persian arz-dasht: widely given (e.g. Mahan Kosh); confirm.
Three-movement summary of the Ardas (opening, remembrance, petition): a teaching simplification; confirm it is acceptable.
